solutions.title: Multiply first
solutions.body:
Multiplication comes before addition: $2 \times 9 = 18$. Then $18 + 200 + 9 = 227$.

**Answer: (E) 227**

solutions.title: Group the numbers
solutions.body:
$2\times 9 + 9$ is three nines, $27$. Add $200$: $227$.

**Answer: (E) 227**

prompt: Four sticks have 8 ends. How many ends do 7 sticks have?

solutions.title: Ends per stick
solutions.body:
4 sticks have 8 ends, so each stick has $8 \div 4 = 2$ ends. 7 sticks have $7 \times 2 = 14$ ends.

**Answer: (E) 14**

solutions.title: Add three more sticks
solutions.body:
Going from 4 to 7 sticks adds 3 sticks, that is $3 \times 2 = 6$ more ends: $8 + 6 = 14$.

**Answer: (E) 14**

prompt: Where is the Kangaroo?

choices.text: In the circle and in the triangle but not in the square.
In the circle and in the square but not in the triangle.
In the triangle and in the square but not in the circle.
In the circle but in neither the square nor the triangle.
In the square but in neither the circle nor the triangle.

solutions.title: Check each shape
solutions.body:
- The kangaroo is inside the circle.
- It is inside the square.
- The triangle's lower edge passes above the kangaroo, so it is **not** in the triangle.

**Answer: (B)**

solutions.title: Rule out choices
solutions.body:
The kangaroo is clearly inside the square, so (A) and (D) are wrong. It is inside the circle, so (C) and (E) are wrong. Only (B) is left, and it fits: the kangaroo is below the triangle.

**Answer: (B)**

prompt: In the picture you see the number 930. How many small squares must be changed so that the number becomes 806?

solutions.title: Compare digit by digit
solutions.body:
Compare each digit of 930 with the digit below it in 806:
- 9 → 8: only the white square at the left of the fourth row must become dark: **1** change.
- 3 → 0: the two white squares on the left of rows 2 and 4 become dark, and the middle square of row 3 becomes white: **3** changes.
- 0 → 6: the middle square of row 3 becomes dark and the right square of row 2 becomes white: **2** changes.

Total: $1 + 3 + 2 = 6$.

**Answer: (B) 6**

solutions.title: Count only the white squares
solutions.body:
Only white squares matter. Mark each white square of 930 and of 806. A square must change if it is white in one number and dark in the other. Doing this for all three digits gives $1 + 3 + 2 = 6$ squares.

**Answer: (B) 6**

prompt: Mother bought 16 mandarins. Karl ate half of them, Eva ate two, and Dana ate the rest. How many mandarins did Dana eat?

solutions.title: Step by step
solutions.body:
Karl ate half of 16, which is 8. That leaves $16 - 8 = 8$. Eva ate 2, so $8 - 2 = 6$ are left for Dana.

**Answer: (B) 6**

solutions.title: Add up and subtract
solutions.body:
Karl and Eva together ate $8 + 2 = 10$. Dana ate $16 - 10 = 6$.

**Answer: (B) 6**

prompt: In his garden Tony made a pathway using 10 paving stones. Each paver was 4 dm wide and 6 dm long. He then drew a black line connecting the middle points of each paving stone, as shown. How long is the black line?

solutions.title: Two kinds of steps
solutions.body:
10 stones give 9 pieces of black line, one between each pair of neighbouring stones.
- When two stones touch along their long sides, their middle points are one width apart: **4 dm**.
- When two stones touch along their short sides, their middle points are one length apart: **6 dm**.

In the picture there are 5 long pieces (6 dm) and 4 short pieces (4 dm): $5 \times 6 + 4 \times 4 = 30 + 16 = 46$ dm.

**Answer: (C) 46 dm**

solutions.title: Check with the choices
solutions.body:
There are 9 pieces, each 4 dm or 6 dm. All 4 dm would give 36 dm and all 6 dm would give 54 dm, so the answer is between them: 40, 46 or 50. The pieces alternate long, short, long, ..., starting and ending with a long piece, so there are 5 long and 4 short pieces: $30 + 16 = 46$ dm.

**Answer: (C) 46 dm**

prompt: Sophie rolled a die four times and scored a total of 23 points. How often did she roll a six?

solutions.title: Start from the biggest total
solutions.body:
Four sixes would give $4 \times 6 = 24$, only 1 more than 23. So one roll was a 5 instead of a 6: $6 + 6 + 6 + 5 = 23$. She rolled a six 3 times.

**Answer: (D) 3**

solutions.title: Why not fewer sixes?
solutions.body:
With only two sixes, the other two rolls are at most $5 + 5 = 10$, giving at most $12 + 10 = 22 < 23$. With four sixes the total is 24. So there must be exactly three sixes.

**Answer: (D) 3**

prompt: A certain film lasts 90 minutes. It begins at 17:10. During the film there are two advert breaks, one lasting eight minutes and the other five minutes. At what time will the film end?

solutions.title: Total time
solutions.body:
Film plus breaks: $90 + 8 + 5 = 103$ minutes = 1 hour 43 minutes. $17{:}10 + 1{:}43 = 18{:}53$.

**Answer: (D) at 18:53**

solutions.title: Add in pieces
solutions.body:
17:10 + 90 minutes = 18:40. Add 8 minutes: 18:48. Add 5 minutes: 18:53.

**Answer: (D) at 18:53**

prompt: In a dance group there are 25 boys and 19 girls. Every week 2 more boys and 3 more girls join the group. After how many weeks will there be the same number of boys as girls in the dance group?

solutions.title: Close the gap
solutions.body:
At the start there are $25 - 19 = 6$ more boys. Each week the girls catch up by $3 - 2 = 1$. So it takes 6 weeks.

**Answer: (A) 6**

solutions.title: Make a table
solutions.body:
Week 0: 25 boys, 19 girls. Week 1: 27, 22. Week 2: 29, 25. Week 3: 31, 28. Week 4: 33, 31. Week 5: 35, 34. Week 6: 37, 37.

**Answer: (A) 6**

prompt: Peter shared a bar of chocolate. First he broke off a row with five pieces for his brother (Bruder). Then he broke off a column with 7 pieces for his sister (Schwester). How many pieces were there in the entire bar of chocolate?

solutions.title: Find the size of the bar
solutions.body:
The row has 5 pieces, so the bar is 5 pieces wide. After that row was gone, a column had 7 pieces, so 7 rows were left. Together with the brother's row the bar had 8 rows of 5 pieces: $8 \times 5 = 40$.

**Answer: (D) 40**

solutions.title: Draw it
solutions.body:
Draw a rectangle 5 squares wide. Remove the top row. A column of the rest has 7 squares, so the whole column (with the removed row) had 8 squares. $5 \times 8 = 40$.

**Answer: (D) 40**

prompt: A farmer has 30 cows, some chickens and no other animals. The total number of chickens' legs is equal to the total number of cows' legs. How many animals does the farmer have?

solutions.title: Count legs
solutions.body:
Cows' legs: $30 \times 4 = 120$. The chickens also have 120 legs, so there are $120 \div 2 = 60$ chickens. Animals: $30 + 60 = 90$.

**Answer: (B) 90**

solutions.title: Compare one cow with chickens
solutions.body:
One cow has as many legs as two chickens. So there are twice as many chickens as cows: 60 chickens. $30 + 60 = 90$.

**Answer: (B) 90**

prompt: Picture X is paired with picture Y. Which of the following pictures is paired with picture G?

solutions.title: Find the rule
solutions.body:
Compare X and Y square by square: every square that is dark in X is white in Y, and every white square in X is dark in Y. So the partner is the **colour swap** (negative).

Swap all colours of G: row 1 becomes dark, dark, white, dark; row 2 white, white, dark, dark; row 3 dark, white, white, dark; row 4 dark, dark, dark, white. That is picture (E).

**Answer: (E)**

solutions.title: Count dark squares
solutions.body:
G has 6 dark squares out of 16, so its colour swap must have 10 dark squares. Only pictures with 10 dark squares can work; checking the white squares of (E), they are exactly where G is dark.

**Answer: (E)**

prompt: The length of a rectangle is 8 cm. The width is half as long. How long are the sides of a square that has the same perimeter as the rectangle?

solutions.title: Perimeter
solutions.body:
Width $= 4$ cm. Perimeter $= 8 + 4 + 8 + 4 = 24$ cm. A square has 4 equal sides: $24 \div 4 = 6$ cm.

**Answer: (B) 6 cm**

solutions.title: Average side
solutions.body:
A square with the same perimeter has sides equal to the average of the length and the width: $(8 + 4) \div 2 = 6$ cm.

**Answer: (B) 6 cm**

prompt: Thomas has made a table out of small cubes. How many small cubes did he use?

solutions.title: Table top plus legs
solutions.body:
The table top is one layer: 4 cubes wide and 5 cubes deep (count the rows on the top), so $4 \times 5 = 20$ cubes. Each of the 4 legs has 3 cubes under the top: $4 \times 3 = 12$. Total $20 + 12 = 32$.

**Answer: (D) 32**

solutions.title: Count layer by layer
solutions.body:
Top layer: 20 cubes. Each of the three layers below has one cube in each of the four legs: $3 \times 4 = 12$. $20 + 12 = 32$.

**Answer: (D) 32**

prompt: Three squirrels Anni, Asia and Elli have collected 7 nuts. They have all collected a different amount of nuts, and everybody has collected at least one nut. Anni has collected the least and Asia the most. How many nuts has Elli collected?

solutions.title: List the possibilities
solutions.body:
Three different numbers, each at least 1, adding to 7: $1 + 2 + 4$ is the only way ($1+2+3 = 6$ is too small, $1+3+4 = 8$ is too big, and $1 + 1 + 5$ uses the same number twice). Anni has the least (1), Asia the most (4), so Elli has 2.

**Answer: (B) 2**

solutions.title: Smallest amounts first
solutions.body:
The smallest possible amounts are 1, 2, 3, which make only 6. One more nut must go to Asia (the one with the most), giving 1, 2, 4. If Elli had 3, Asia would need at least 4 and the total would be at least 8. So Elli has 2.

**Answer: (B) 2**

prompt: Which of the following diagrams is impossible to make with the two dominoes?

solutions.title: Watch the slant of the dots
solutions.body:
One domino is 1|2, the other 1|3. On each domino the dots of the 2 and the 3 slant like \ (top-left to bottom-right). When a domino is turned a quarter turn (lying sideways), the slant changes to /; when it is turned upside down it stays \.

In (E) the 3 slants like /, so the 1|3 domino must lie sideways in the bottom row. Then the 1|2 domino must lie sideways in the top row, and its 2 would also slant like /. But in (E) the 2 slants like \. So (E) is impossible. The other four pictures can all be made.

**Answer: (E)**

solutions.title: Try to place the dominoes in (E)
solutions.body:
In (E) the 2 is top-left and the 3 is bottom-right. Either both dominoes stand upright (left column and right column) or both lie flat (top row and bottom row). Upright: the 3 would slant \ but it slants /. Flat: the 2 would slant / but it slants \. Neither works.

**Answer: (E)**

prompt: A white and a black pig weigh together 320 kg. The black pig weighs 32 kg more than the white one. How much does the white pig weigh?

solutions.title: Take away the difference
solutions.body:
Take the extra 32 kg off the black pig: then both pigs weigh the same and together $320 - 32 = 288$ kg. The white pig weighs $288 \div 2 = 144$ kg.

**Answer: (B) 144 kg**

solutions.title: Check from the middle
solutions.body:
If they weighed the same, each would be 160 kg. The black one is 32 kg heavier, so each is 16 kg away from 160: white $= 144$ kg, black $= 176$ kg. Check: $144 + 176 = 320$.

**Answer: (B) 144 kg**

prompt: Anna and Peter live in the same street. On one side of Anna's house there are 27 houses, and on the other side 13 houses. Peter lives in the house right in the middle of the street. How many houses are there between Anna's and Peter's houses?

solutions.title: Number the houses
solutions.body:
There are $27 + 1 + 13 = 41$ houses. The middle house is number 21 (20 houses on each side). Counting from the short end, Anna's house is number 14. The houses between are numbers 15 to 20: 6 houses.

**Answer: (A) 6**

solutions.title: Balance the two sides
solutions.body:
Peter has 20 houses on each side. Anna has only 13 houses on her short side, so Peter is $20 - 13 = 7$ houses further along. That means 6 houses lie strictly between them.

**Answer: (A) 6**

prompt: A secret agent wants to crack a six digit code. He knows that the sum of the digits in the even positions is equal to the sum of the digits in the odd positions. Which of the following numbers is the code? (Each * is a digit that he cannot see.)

solutions.title: Check each choice
solutions.body:
Positions 1, 3, 5 are odd; positions 2, 4, 6 are even. A star can be any digit 0–9.
- (A) 8 1 * * 6 1: odd $= 14 + \ast$, even $= 2 + \ast$. The even sum would need a star 12 bigger: impossible.
- (B) 7 * 7 2 7 *: odd $= 21$, even $= 2 + \ast + \ast \le 20$: impossible.
- (C) 4 * 4 1 4 1: odd $= 12$, even $= \ast + 2$, so the star would be 10: impossible.
- (D) 1 2 * 9 * 8: even $= 19$, odd $= 1 + \ast + \ast$, works with both stars 9 (code 129998).
- (E) 1 8 1 * 2 *: odd $= 4$, even $\ge 8$: impossible.

**Answer: (D)**

solutions.title: Look for big gaps
solutions.body:
In every choice except (D), the known digits already make one sum too big for the stars to fix. In (D) the stars can be 9 and 9: $1 + 9 + 9 = 19 = 2 + 9 + 8$.

**Answer: (D)**

prompt: Meta collects pictures of famous sports people. Each year she collects as many pictures as she did in the previous two years. In 2008 she had 60 photos and this year (2009) she has 96. How many photos did she have in 2006?

solutions.title: Work backwards
solutions.body:
The number for a year is the sum of the two years before.
- 2009: $96 = 60 + (\text{2007})$, so 2007 had 36.
- 2008: $60 = 36 + (\text{2006})$, so 2006 had 24.

**Answer: (B) 24**

prompt: In a vase there is one red, one blue, one yellow and one white flower. Maja the bee visits each flower exactly once. She begins with the red flower and she never flies directly from the yellow to the white flower. In how many different ways can she visit each flower?

solutions.title: List all orders
solutions.body:
After red, the other three flowers (blue B, yellow Y, white W) can come in 6 orders: BYW, BWY, YBW, YWB, WBY, WYB. The orders BYW and YWB have yellow directly followed by white, so they are not allowed. $6 - 2 = 4$.

**Answer: (D) 4**

solutions.title: Count the forbidden ones
solutions.body:
Treat 'yellow then white' as one block. Then after red we arrange the block and blue: 2 ways. So 2 of the 6 orders are forbidden and $6 - 2 = 4$ remain.

**Answer: (D) 4**

prompt: In a haunted house the house ghost suddenly disappears. At that moment in time all clocks show 6:15 o'clock. However, there is also one strange clock in the house that shows the correct time before that event. Starting from the disappearance it starts to count backwards. At 19:30 o'clock according to the real time the house ghost reappears. What time does the odd clock show at that time?

solutions.title: Time passed
solutions.body:
The ghost disappeared at 18:15 (6:15 in the evening) and came back at 19:30, which is 1 hour 15 minutes later. The strange clock runs backwards for 1 hour 15 minutes from 18:15: $18{:}15 - 1{:}15 = 17{:}00$.

**Answer: (A) 17:00**

solutions.title: Mirror around 18:15
solutions.body:
19:30 is 75 minutes after 18:15. Going 75 minutes before 18:15 gives 17:00.

**Answer: (A) 17:00**

prompt: Sylvia draws shapes made up of straight lines which are each 1 cm long. At the end of each line she continues in a right angle either to the left or right. At every turn she notes down either a ♥ or a ♠ on a piece of paper. The same symbol always indicates a turn in the same direction. Today her notes show ♥♠♠♠♥♥. Which of the following shapes could she have drawn today if A indicates her starting point?

solutions.title: Follow shape (E)
solutions.body:
Start at A and walk up. Turns: right, left, left, left, right, right. That is one turn, then three of the other kind, then two of the first kind — exactly the pattern ♥♠♠♠♥♥ with ♥ = right and ♠ = left.

**Answer: (E)**

solutions.title: Rule out others
solutions.body:
The pattern has 6 turns, so the shape has 7 lines, and the turns go: one way once, the other way three times in a row, then the first way twice. Three turns in a row in the same direction make three sides of a small square. Walking the other shapes from A gives different turn patterns (for example (C) alternates left and right in pairs). Only (E) matches.

**Answer: (E)**

prompt: In Funny-Foot-Land men and women wear the same sort of shoes. Each man has a left foot that is two sizes bigger than the right foot. Each woman has a left foot that is one size bigger than the right foot. However, shoes are only sold in pairs of the same size. To save money some friends decide to buy shoes together. After putting on their new shoes two shoes are left over – one of size 36 and one of size 45. What is the minimum number of people in that group?

solutions.title: Make a chain
solutions.body:
Each pair bought has a left and a right shoe of the same size. Follow a chain: the leftover 36 is a left shoe; its right shoe goes to a person with right foot 36. That person's left foot is 37 or 38, so another pair of that size is bought, and its right shoe goes to the next person, and so on. Each person moves the size up by 1 (woman) or 2 (man). The chain must climb from 36 to 45, which is 9 sizes, and ends with the right shoe of size 45 left over.

With steps of at most 2 we need at least 5 people ($4$ people climb at most 8). Five works: 4 men and 1 woman: $36 \to 38 \to 40 \to 42 \to 44 \to 45$.

**Answer: (A) 5**

solutions.title: Fewest steps
solutions.body:
We need to add steps of 1 or 2 to go from 36 to 45 (a total of 9). As few steps as possible: $2 + 2 + 2 + 2 + 1 = 9$ uses 5 steps, and 4 steps make at most 8. Each step is one person, so at least 5 people.

**Answer: (A) 5**

prompt: In the picture you see a map. In the middle a piece is missing. The cat should be able to reach the milk, and the mouse the cheese, but the cat and the mouse must not meet each other. What should the piece in the middle look like?

solutions.title: Follow the roads
solutions.body:
The cat's road comes into the middle piece from the **left**, and the road to the milk leaves it at the **top**. The mouse's road comes in from the **right**, and the road to the cheese leaves at the **bottom**. So the piece must join left to top and right to bottom, with the two roads not touching. Piece (E) has exactly these two curved roads.

**Answer: (E)**

solutions.title: Rule out the others
solutions.body:
Pieces (B) and (D) let all four roads meet in the middle, so the cat could meet the mouse. Pieces (A) and (C) join the wrong sides (for example left with right), so the cat could not reach the milk. Only (E) works.

**Answer: (E)**

prompt: A 40 minute long lesson began at 11:50. Exactly in the middle of the lesson a bird flew into the classroom. At what time did this happen?

solutions.title: Half of the lesson
solutions.body:
The middle of a 40-minute lesson is after 20 minutes. 11:50 + 20 minutes = 12:10.

**Answer: (C) 12:10**

solutions.title: Find the end first
solutions.body:
The lesson ends at 11:50 + 40 min = 12:30. Halfway between 11:50 and 12:30 is 12:10.

**Answer: (C) 12:10**

prompt: Which square contains 3 quadrilaterals, 3 circles and 4 hearts?

solutions.title: Count each picture
solutions.body:
Count the shapes in each square:
- (A): 3 squares, 4 circles, 4 hearts.
- (B): 3 squares, 4 circles, 3 hearts.
- (C): 2 squares, 4 circles, 4 hearts.
- (D): 3 squares, 3 circles, 4 hearts ✓.
- (E): 3 squares, 5 circles, 4 hearts.

**Answer: (D)**

solutions.title: Start with the circles
solutions.body:
Circles are the quickest to check: (A), (B) and (C) have 4 circles and (E) has 5. Only (D) has 3 circles, and it also has 3 squares and 4 hearts.

**Answer: (D)**

prompt: In a cafe the soup costs €4, the main course €9 and the dessert €5. The three courses when ordered together cost €15. How many euros cheaper is this than ordering the same three courses separately?

solutions.title: Add and compare
solutions.body:
Separately: $4 + 9 + 5 = 18$ euros. Together: 15 euros. Saving: $18 - 15 = 3$ euros.

**Answer: (A) €3**

solutions.title: Compare with the main course
solutions.body:
Main course and soup already cost 13 euros, so for 15 euros the dessert costs only 2 euros instead of 5. That saves 3 euros.

**Answer: (A) €3**

prompt: Six coins build a triangle (see picture). What is the smallest number of coins that must be moved to create the circle?

solutions.title: Keep four coins
solutions.body:
The circle (ring) has 3 rows of 2 coins: the middle row is wider. Put the ring over the triangle so that its top row is the triangle's second row (2 coins) and its middle row uses the two outer coins of the bottom row. These 4 coins stay. Move the top coin and the middle coin of the bottom row to make the ring's bottom row. That is 2 moves.

**Answer: (B) 2**

solutions.title: Why one move is not enough
solutions.body:
In the ring no three coins lie in a touching straight row, and no three coins all touch each other. In the triangle the bottom row is a straight row of 3, and the top coin with the two coins below it all touch each other. Moving one coin can break only one of these two groups (they share no coin), so at least 2 moves are needed — and 2 moves work.

**Answer: (B) 2**

prompt: Four friends each eat some ice cream. Mike eats more than Franz, Jaroslav eats more than Veit and Jaroslav eats less than Franz. Put the friends in order according to how much ice cream they have eaten. Begin with the largest amount.

solutions.title: Chain the facts
solutions.body:
Mike > Franz. Franz > Jaroslav (Jaroslav eats less than Franz). Jaroslav > Veit. So Mike > Franz > Jaroslav > Veit.

**Answer: (C) Mike, Franz, Jaroslav, Veit**

solutions.title: Check the choices
solutions.body:
Veit eats less than Jaroslav, so Veit cannot be first: (B) is out. Franz eats more than Jaroslav, so Franz cannot be last: (A), (D) and (E) are out. Only (C) is left, and it fits all three facts.

**Answer: (C)**

prompt: I have tiles that look like this (see picture). Which pattern can I not create with them?

solutions.title: Where can the line go?
solutions.body:
Every tile is a square with one thick line along a **diagonal**. In (B) the tiles are turned to stand on a corner, so a tile's diagonal would be horizontal or vertical. But the thick lines in (B) are slanted — they run along the edges of the tiles, not along diagonals. So (B) cannot be made.

**Answer: (B)**

solutions.title: Check the others
solutions.body:
(A) and (C): square tiles, each with a diagonal. (D) and (E): tiles turned on a corner, whose diagonals are the horizontal/vertical thick lines that are drawn. All of these are possible; only (B) has lines that no tile has.

**Answer: (B)**

prompt: Eva is a centipede with exactly 100 feet. Yesterday she bought 16 pairs of shoes and wore them straight away. Even so she still had 14 feet with no shoes. On how many feet did she already wear shoes before going shopping yesterday?

solutions.title: Count the shoes now
solutions.body:
Now $100 - 14 = 86$ feet have shoes. The new shoes: 16 pairs $= 32$ shoes. So before shopping $86 - 32 = 54$ feet wore shoes.

**Answer: (C) 54**

solutions.title: Check
solutions.body:
54 old shoes + 32 new shoes = 86 feet with shoes, plus 14 bare feet = 100. ✓

**Answer: (C) 54**

prompt: Given that $\blacktriangle + \blacktriangle + 6 = \blacktriangle + \blacktriangle + \blacktriangle + \blacktriangle$. Which number should replace $\blacktriangle$?

solutions.title: Take away equal things
solutions.body:
Remove two triangles from both sides: $6 = \blacktriangle + \blacktriangle$. So $\blacktriangle = 3$.

**Answer: (B) 3**

prompt: Maria folds a square piece of paper in such a way that the kangaroos exactly overlap each other. Along how many of the lines shown is this possible?

solutions.title: Test each line
solutions.body:
Four lines are drawn: the vertical middle line, the horizontal middle line and the two diagonals.
- The left half is a mirror picture of the right half, so folding along the **vertical** line works.
- The top half is a mirror picture of the bottom half, so folding along the **horizontal** line works.
- Along a diagonal, a kangaroo's head would land on a tail or a body, so the diagonals do not work.

That makes 2 lines.

**Answer: (C) 2**

solutions.title: Look at one kangaroo
solutions.body:
Take the top-left kangaroo. Folding along the diagonal through its corner would fold it onto itself, but it is not symmetric about that diagonal (its ears are on one side and its face on the other). Folding along the other diagonal sends it to the bottom-right kangaroo, which faces the wrong way. The two middle lines send it onto the top-right and bottom-left kangaroos, which are exact mirror pictures.

**Answer: (C) 2**

prompt: Matthias and Klara live in a tower block. Klara lives 12 floors above Matthias. One day Matthias climbs the staircase to visit Klara. When halfway he is on the 8th floor. On which floor does Klara live?

solutions.title: Half of 12
solutions.body:
Halfway is 6 floors above Matthias and 6 floors below Klara. So Klara lives on floor $8 + 6 = 14$.

**Answer: (B) 14th**

solutions.title: Find Matthias first
solutions.body:
Matthias lives on floor $8 - 6 = 2$. Klara lives 12 floors higher: $2 + 12 = 14$.

**Answer: (B) 14th**

prompt: A large cube is made from 64 small cubes. The 5 visible faces of the large cube are green, the bottom face is red. How many of the small cubes have 3 green faces?

solutions.title: Look at the corners
solutions.body:
A small cube can only show 3 faces of the big cube if it is at a **corner**. The big cube has 8 corners. The 4 bottom corners each have one red face, so only 2 green faces. The 4 top corners have 3 green faces (top and two sides).

**Answer: (A) 4**

solutions.title: Edges are not enough
solutions.body:
Cubes in the middle of an edge show only 2 faces, cubes in the middle of a face show 1. So we only need the 8 corners, and only the 4 top ones have no red face.

**Answer: (A) 4**

prompt: Kangi walks directly from the zoo to school (Schule) and counts the flowers along the way. Which of the following numbers can he not obtain this way?

solutions.title: List all routes
solutions.body:
Count the flowers: first loop: top path 1, bottom path 2. Middle path: 3. Second loop: top path 8, bottom path 5.

Routes: $1 + 3 + 8 = 12$, $1 + 3 + 5 = 9$, $2 + 3 + 8 = 13$, $2 + 3 + 5 = 10$. The number 11 is not possible.

**Answer: (C) 11**

solutions.title: Think about the second loop
solutions.body:
Every route collects 3 flowers in the middle. To get 11 he would need $8$ more from the two loops: with 8 on the second loop he needs 0 on the first (impossible), with 5 he needs 3 on the first (but the first loop offers only 1 or 2).

**Answer: (C) 11**

prompt: A ferry boat can transport, in one journey, either 10 cars or 6 lorries. Yesterday the boat crossed the river 5 times. It was always fully loaded and transported a total of 42 vehicles. How many of these were cars?

solutions.title: Try the number of car trips
solutions.body:
If all 5 trips carried lorries: 30 vehicles. Each trip with cars instead of lorries adds 4 vehicles. We need $42 - 30 = 12$ more, so 3 trips carried cars: $3 \times 10 = 30$ cars (and 2 trips with 12 lorries).

**Answer: (E) 30**

prompt: Hans began a chain-email. He sent an e-mail to his friend Peter, who sent it on to 2 more people. Each person that receives the e-mail should send it to 2 more people. After 3 rounds $1 + 2 + 4 = 7$ people have received the e-mail. How many people have received the e-mail after 5 rounds?

solutions.title: Keep doubling
solutions.body:
Each round twice as many new people get the e-mail: 1, 2, 4, 8, 16. After 5 rounds: $1 + 2 + 4 + 8 + 16 = 31$.

**Answer: (C) 31**

solutions.title: Pattern of totals
solutions.body:
Totals after each round: 1, 3, 7, 15, 31 — each total is one less than a doubling number (2, 4, 8, 16, 32).

**Answer: (C) 31**

prompt: On the playground some children measure the length of the playground with their strides. Anni makes 15 strides, Betty 17, Denis 12 and Ivo 14. Who has the longest stride?

solutions.title: Fewer steps means longer steps
solutions.body:
They all walk the same length. Whoever needs the fewest strides must have the longest stride. Denis needs only 12.

**Answer: (C) Denis**

solutions.title: Imagine a number
solutions.body:
Suppose the playground is 60 m long. Denis: $60 \div 12 = 5$ m per stride; Anni $60 \div 15 = 4$ m; Ivo and Betty even less. Denis's stride is the longest.

**Answer: (C) Denis**

prompt: Which number must replace the question mark, if the total of the numbers in each row is the same?

solutions.title: Compare column by column
solutions.body:
Each number in the second row (11 to 20) is 10 more than the number above it. That is $10 \times 10 = 100$ more in total. To make the sums equal, the question mark must be 100 less than 199: $199 - 100 = 99$.

**Answer: (A) 99**

prompt: The number $60 \times 60 \times 24 \times 7$ is the same as

choices.text: The number of minutes in seven weeks
The number of hours in sixty days
The number of seconds in seven hours
The number of seconds in one week
The number of minutes in 24 weeks

solutions.title: Read the factors
solutions.body:
60 seconds in a minute, 60 minutes in an hour, 24 hours in a day, 7 days in a week. So $60 \times 60 \times 24 \times 7$ is the number of seconds in one week.

**Answer: (D)**

solutions.title: Check another choice
solutions.body:
Minutes in seven weeks would be $60 \times 24 \times 7 \times 7$ — not the same. Seconds in seven hours would be $60 \times 60 \times 7$, much smaller.

**Answer: (D)**

prompt: Two years ago the cats Tim and Tom were together 15 years old. Now Tom is 13 years old. In how many years will Tim be 9 years old?

solutions.title: Ages two years ago
solutions.body:
Two years ago Tom was 11, so Tim was $15 - 11 = 4$. Now Tim is 6. He will be 9 in 3 years.

**Answer: (C) 3**

solutions.title: Ages now
solutions.body:
Now the two cats are together $15 + 2 + 2 = 19$ years old. Tim is $19 - 13 = 6$, so 9 in 3 years.

**Answer: (C) 3**

prompt: Kamilla wrote down all of the numbers from 1 to 100 one after the other in a table with 5 columns. A part of the table is shown. Her brother cut out a piece of the table and erased some of the numbers. Which of the following could this piece have been?

solutions.title: Column of a number
solutions.body:
Each piece is 5 cells wide, like the table, so its cells are exactly the columns 1–5. A number's column is given by its last digit: 1 or 6 → column 1, 2 or 7 → 2, 3 or 8 → 3, 4 or 9 → 4, 5 or 0 → 5. The number below a number is 5 more.
- (A): 43 and 48 are both in column 3, but drawn in different columns.
- (B): 52 comes before 58, so it can't be in the row below.
- (C): 69 is in column 4 and the row below holds 71–75, with 72 in column 2 ✓.
- (D): 81 belongs in column 1, not column 2.
- (E): 90 belongs in column 5.

**Answer: (C)**

solutions.title: Fill in the piece
solutions.body:
Fill in piece (C): the top row would be 66, 67, 68, **69**, 70 and the bottom row 71, **72**, 73, 74, 75 — this matches. Filling in the others always leads to a contradiction (for (A) the top row would be 42, 43, 44, 45, 46 and the cell below 44 would be 49, not 48).

**Answer: (C)**

prompt: The teacher said: "In our school library there are roughly 2010 books." The pupils then guessed exactly how many there are. Artur guesses 2010, Beate 1998 and Carlos 2015. They are wrong by 12, 7 and 5, but not in this order. How many books are in the library?

solutions.title: Test the choices
solutions.body:
For 2003: Artur is off by 7, Beate by 5, Carlos by 12. These are 12, 7, 5 in a different order ✓. (Check 2005: 5, 7, 10 — no; 2022: 12, 24, 7 — no.)

**Answer: (A) 2003**

solutions.title: Use the biggest guess
solutions.body:
Beate (1998) and Carlos (2015) are 17 apart. Two of the errors must add up to 17 if the answer lies between them: $12 + 5 = 17$. So the answer is 1998 + 5 = 2003 or 1998 + 12 = 2010. 2010 would make Artur off by 0, so it is 2003 (Artur off by 7).

**Answer: (A) 2003**

prompt: Lines are drawn on a piece of paper and some of the lines are given numbers. The paper is cut along some of these lines and then folded as shown in the picture. What is the total of the numbers on the lines that were cut?

solutions.title: One cut per corner square
solutions.body:
The paper is a $3 \times 3$ grid. After folding, the middle square and the four squares next to it lie flat as a cross, and each of the four corner squares is folded up or down. A corner square that is folded must be cut along one of its two numbered lines and stay joined along the other. The corner squares are bounded by the pairs 1–2, 3–4, 5–6 and 7–8.

In the picture the four flaps go round like a pinwheel: each flap hangs from the arm on the same side (turning the same way around the centre). That means the cuts are 2, 4, 6 and 8 (cutting 1, 3, 5, 7 would make the mirror-image pinwheel). Total: $2 + 4 + 6 + 8 = 20$.

**Answer: (D) 20**

solutions.title: Which totals are possible?
solutions.body:
One line from each pair is cut, so the total is between $1 + 3 + 5 + 7 = 16$ and $2 + 4 + 6 + 8 = 20$; 21 is impossible. The flaps all turn the same way round, so either all odd lines or all even lines were cut. The picture shows the even ones cut.

**Answer: (D) 20**

prompt:
Andrew, Stefan, Robert and Marko meet each other at a concert in Zagreb. They come from different cities: Paris, Dubrovnik, Rome and Berlin (not necessarily in this order).
- Andrew and the friend from Berlin arrive first in Zagreb. Neither of the two has been to Paris or Rome.
- Robert is not from Berlin, but he arrives with the friend from Paris.
- Marko and the friend from Paris enjoyed the concert very much.

From which city does Marko come?

solutions.title: Place each friend
solutions.body:
- Andrew is not the friend from Berlin and has never been to Paris or Rome, so Andrew is from **Dubrovnik**.
- Robert is not from Berlin and not from Paris (he arrives *with* the Paris friend), so Robert is from **Rome**.
- Marko is not from Paris (he enjoyed the concert *with* the Paris friend), so Marko is from **Berlin**, and Stefan is from Paris.

**Answer: (D) Berlin**

solutions.title: Table
solutions.body:
Make a 4 × 4 table of friends and cities and cross out: Andrew–Berlin, Andrew–Paris, Andrew–Rome, Robert–Berlin, Robert–Paris, Marko–Paris. Andrew must be Dubrovnik; then Robert must be Rome; then Marko must be Berlin. (Zagreb is where the concert is, not a home city.)

**Answer: (D) Berlin**

prompt: Berti's friends add together the day and the month of their birthdays. They each get the answer 35, but no two have the same birthday. What is the maximum number of friends Berti has?

solutions.title: Go month by month
solutions.body:
Day $= 35 -$ month.
- January: day 34, February: 33, March: 32, April: 31 — none of these exist (April has 30 days).
- May 30, June 29, July 28, August 27, September 26, October 25, November 24, December 23 all exist.

That is 8 possible birthdays.

**Answer: (B) 8**

solutions.title: Largest day is 31
solutions.body:
The day is at most 31, so the month is at least 4. April 31 doesn't exist, so the months 5 to 12 work: 8 months, one birthday each.

**Answer: (B) 8**

prompt: Bernd wants to paint the word KANGAROO. He begins on a Wednesday and paints one letter each day. On which day will he paint the last letter?

solutions.title: Count the letters
solutions.body:
KANGAROO has 8 letters, so he paints on 8 days. Day 1 is Wednesday; 7 days later, day 8, is again a Wednesday.

**Answer: (C) Wednesday**

solutions.title: List the days
solutions.body:
K Wed, A Thu, N Fri, G Sat, A Sun, R Mon, O Tue, O Wed.

**Answer: (C) Wednesday**

prompt: Which stone should Mr Flintstone place on the right side of the scales, so that both sides weigh the same?

solutions.title: Add both sides
solutions.body:
Left side: $26 + 8 + 12 = 46$ kg. Right side: $20 + 17 = 37$ kg. The missing stone must weigh $46 - 37 = 9$ kg: stone (C).

**Answer: (C) the 9 kg stone**

solutions.title: Pair up stones
solutions.body:
Compare $26$ with $20$: left is 6 more. Compare $12$ with $17$: right is 5 more. So far left is 1 more, plus the 8 kg stone: left is 9 kg heavier.

**Answer: (C) the 9 kg stone**

prompt: A game is played on a board as shown in the picture. I move the counter from square to square according to the following rules. First, one square to the right, then one square up, then one square left, then one square down, and then once again one square right. Which picture shows where the counter can then be found?

solutions.title: Moves that cancel
solutions.body:
Right then left cancel each other; up then down cancel each other. What is left is the final 'one square right'. So the counter ends one square to the right of where it started, in the same row: picture (B).

**Answer: (B)**

solutions.title: Walk it step by step
solutions.body:
Starting square → right → up → left (now right above the start) → down (back on the start) → right. The counter is one square right of the start.

**Answer: (B)**

prompt: Simon awoke one and a half hours ago. In three and a half hours he will catch a train to go to his grandma. How long before the time his train leaves did he wake up?

solutions.title: Add the two times
solutions.body:
From waking up until now: $1\frac{1}{2}$ hours. From now until the train: $3\frac{1}{2}$ hours. Together $1\frac{1}{2} + 3\frac{1}{2} = 5$ hours.

**Answer: (E) Five hours**

solutions.title: Use a clock
solutions.body:
Say it is 10:00 now. He woke at 8:30 and the train leaves at 13:30. From 8:30 to 13:30 is 5 hours.

**Answer: (E) Five hours**

prompt: Maria describes one of these five shapes in the following way: "It is not a square. It is grey. It is either round or three sided." Which shape did she describe?

solutions.title: Use the clues one by one
solutions.body:
Grey shapes: A (square), B (triangle) and E (rectangle). Not a square: A is out. Round or three-sided: the rectangle E is out. Only the grey triangle B is left.

**Answer: (B) B**

solutions.title: Start with the shape
solutions.body:
Round or three-sided: the triangle B or the circle D. The circle D is white, so it must be B, which is grey and not a square.

**Answer: (B) B**

prompt: Lenka paid 1 euro and 50 cents for three scoops of ice cream. Miso paid 2 euros and 40 cents for two chocolate bars. How much did Igor pay for one scoop of ice cream and one chocolate bar?

solutions.title: Find each price
solutions.body:
One scoop: 150 cents ÷ 3 = 50 cents. One bar: 240 cents ÷ 2 = 120 cents. Together $50 + 120 = 170$ cents = 1 € 70 c.

**Answer: (A) 1 € 70 c**

prompt: The bell of a clocktower rings every full hour (8:00, 9:00, 10:00 etc.) and rings as many times as the number of hours. It also rings once on every half hour (8:30, 9:30, 10:30 etc). How often will it ring between 7:55 and 10:45?

solutions.title: Full hours and half hours
solutions.body:
Full hours in the time: 8, 9, 10, giving $27$ rings. Half hours: 8:30, 9:30, 10:30, giving 3 rings. $27 + 3 = 30$.

**Answer: (D) 30 times**

prompt: Which shape has the biggest area?

solutions.title: Count squares and half squares
solutions.body:
Count whole grid squares, and count two half squares (triangles cut by a diagonal) as one square:
- (A): 10 squares.
- (B): 11 squares.
- (C): 12 squares.
- (D): a $4 \times 2$ rectangle (8) plus a point (1): 9 squares.
- (E): a $2 \times 4$ rectangle (8) plus a point (1): 9 squares.

**Answer: (C)**

solutions.title: Cut and move pieces
solutions.body:
In (C), the four triangular points can be moved to fill a $2 \times 2$ square in the middle plus a ring around it — it fits exactly 12 squares. (D) and (E) are clearly only 9 squares, and (A) and (B) are like (C) with pieces missing.

**Answer: (C)**

prompt: A chicken farmer packs eggs in boxes of 6 and boxes of 12. What is the smallest number of boxes he needs to pack 66 eggs?

solutions.title: Use big boxes first
solutions.body:
Five boxes of 12 hold 60 eggs, and the last 6 eggs go in one small box: $5 + 1 = 6$ boxes.

**Answer: (B) 6**

solutions.title: Why not 5?
solutions.body:
Five boxes hold at most $5 \times 12 = 60 < 66$ eggs. So 6 boxes is the least.

**Answer: (B) 6**

prompt: All the children in a class at school have at least one pet, and at most two pets. They write down how many pets they have together. Two children each have a dog and a fish. Three have each a cat and a dog. No child has two cats. Altogether they have eight cats, six dogs, and two fish. How many children are in the class?

solutions.title: Account for the pets
solutions.body:
- 2 children with dog + fish: uses 2 dogs and both fish.
- 3 children with cat + dog: uses 3 cats and 3 dogs.
- Dogs left: $6 - 5 = 1$, held by 1 more child (only that dog).
- Cats left: $8 - 3 = 5$. No child has two cats, and no fish or dogs are left to pair them with, so 5 children with one cat each.

Total: $2 + 3 + 1 + 5 = 11$.

**Answer: (A) 11**

solutions.title: Count pets per child
solutions.body:
There are $8 + 6 + 2 = 16$ pets. The 5 children with two pets have 10 of them. The other 6 pets (5 cats and 1 dog) must each belong to a different child, because no pairs are possible. $5 + 6 = 11$ children.

**Answer: (A) 11**

prompt: Johannes has only 5 cent coins and 10 cent coins in his pocket. Altogether he has 13 coins. Which of the following amounts cannot be the total of his coins?

solutions.title: Smallest possible total
solutions.body:
The least he can have is 13 coins of 5 c: $13 \times 5 = 65$ c. So 60 c is impossible.

**Answer: (B) 60 c**

solutions.title: Check the others
solutions.body:
Each 10 c coin instead of a 5 c coin adds 5 c, so every multiple of 5 from 65 c to 130 c works: 70 c (1 ten), 80 c (3 tens), 115 c (10 tens), 125 c (12 tens). Only 60 c is below the minimum.

**Answer: (B) 60 c**

prompt: A page is folded along the thick line as shown. Which letter will not be covered by a grey square?

solutions.title: Mirror the grey squares
solutions.body:
Folding flips the left side onto the right like a mirror: the column next to the line lands on the first column to the right, the second column on the second, the third on the third.
- Row 2: grey in columns 2 and 3 on the left → covers B and A.
- Row 4: grey in columns 3 and 2 counted from the line → covers D and the square next to it.
- Row 5: grey in the third column from the line → covers C.

In row 5 the second column from the line on the left is white, so E stays uncovered.

**Answer: (E) E**

solutions.title: Check E directly
solutions.body:
E is in the bottom row, second square to the right of the line. The square that lands on it is the bottom row, second square to the left of the line, which is white. So E is not covered.

**Answer: (E) E**

prompt: Anna, Bob, Cleo, Dido, Eva, and Ferdl each roll a die. Each person rolls a different number. Anna's number is twice as big as Bob's. Anna's number is three times as big as Cleo's. Dido's number is four times as big as Eva's. Which number did Ferdl roll?

solutions.title: Use the multiples
solutions.body:
Anna's number is a multiple of 2 and of 3, so it is 6. Then Bob has 3 and Cleo has 2. Dido is 4 times Eva: only $4 = 4 \times 1$ works. The numbers 6, 3, 2, 4, 1 are used, so Ferdl rolled 5.

**Answer: (D) 5**

solutions.title: Who can roll 5?
solutions.body:
5 is not double, triple or four times any die number, and neither $5 \times 2$, $5 \times 3$ nor $5 \times 4$ is on a die. So 5 cannot be rolled by Anna, Bob, Cleo, Dido or Eva — it must be Ferdl's.

**Answer: (D) 5**

prompt: A quiz show has the following rules: Each contestant begins with 10 points. They must answer 10 questions. For each correct answer they get a point and for each incorrect answer they lose a point. Mrs Blandorfer finished the show with 14 points. How many questions had she answered incorrectly?

solutions.title: Correct minus wrong
solutions.body:
She gained 4 points overall, so (correct) − (wrong) = 4 and (correct) + (wrong) = 10. That gives 7 correct and 3 wrong.

**Answer: (D) 3**

solutions.title: Start from all correct
solutions.body:
All 10 correct would give 20 points. Each wrong answer changes +1 into −1, costing 2 points. $20 - 14 = 6$ points lost, so $6 \div 2 = 3$ wrong answers.

**Answer: (D) 3**

prompt: In each square of the maze there is a piece of cheese. Ronnie the mouse wants to enter and leave the maze as shown in the picture. He doesn't want to visit a square more than once, but would like to eat as much cheese as possible. What is the maximum number of pieces of cheese that he can eat?

solutions.title: Find a long path and the blocked parts
solutions.body:
Number the rows 1–7 from the top and the columns 1–7 from the left; Ronnie enters at the top-left square and leaves at the bottom-right square.

Some parts of the maze are dead ends (pockets with only one opening): if Ronnie goes in, he has to come out through the same square, which is not allowed. Exploring the maze, the best route visits these squares:

row 1 col 1 → down to row 2 → right along row 2 to col 4 → down to row 4 → left to col 3 → up to row 3 → left to col 2 → down to row 4 → left to col 1 → down to row 6 → right → down to row 7 → right to col 3 → up to row 5 → right along row 5 to col 6 → up to row 3 → left to col 5 → up to row 1 → right to col 7 → down column 7 to row 6 → left → down → right to the exit.

That is 37 squares. The 12 squares it misses lie in side branches: going into any of them would either trap Ronnie in a dead end or cut him off from the rest of his route, so no path can collect more than 37 pieces.

**Answer: (C) 37**

prompt: During a party, two identical cakes were each cut into four identical pieces. Each of these pieces was then cut into three identical pieces. Each person at the party got a piece of cake, and there were three pieces left over. How many people were at the party?

solutions.title: Count the pieces
solutions.body:
Each cake: $4 \times 3 = 12$ pieces. Two cakes: 24 pieces. 3 were left, so $24 - 3 = 21$ people.

**Answer: (B) 21**

solutions.title: Draw it
solutions.body:
Draw a cake cut into 4, then each quarter into 3: 12 pieces. Double for two cakes: 24. Cross out 3 leftover pieces: 21.

**Answer: (B) 21**

prompt: Four friends Masha, Sasha, Dasha and Pasha are sitting on a bench. At first Masha swapped places with Dasha. Then Dasha swapped places with Pasha. After this the four friends are sitting from left to right in the order: Masha, Sasha, Dasha, Pasha. In what order, from left to right, were they sitting to begin with?

solutions.title: Undo the swaps backwards
solutions.body:
End: Masha, Sasha, Dasha, Pasha.
- Undo the Dasha–Pasha swap: Masha, Sasha, **Pasha, Dasha**.
- Undo the Masha–Dasha swap: **Dasha**, Sasha, Pasha, **Masha**.

**Answer: (C) Dasha, Sasha, Pasha, Masha**

solutions.title: Check forwards
solutions.body:
Start: Dasha, Sasha, Pasha, Masha. Masha↔Dasha: Masha, Sasha, Pasha, Dasha. Dasha↔Pasha: Masha, Sasha, Dasha, Pasha ✓.

**Answer: (C)**

prompt: How often in a day does a digital clock display four identical digits? The picture shows a digital clock that is displaying exactly two different digits.

solutions.title: List them
solutions.body:
The clock goes from 00:00 to 23:59. Four equal digits: 00:00, 11:11, 22:22. (33:33, 44:44, ... are not times.)

**Answer: (C) 3 times**

solutions.title: Look at the hours
solutions.body:
The hour must be two equal digits: 00, 11 or 22 (33 and above don't exist). The minutes must repeat the same digit, and 00, 11, 22 are all valid minutes. So 3 times.

**Answer: (C) 3 times**

prompt: Four identical dice were put together to make a tower as shown. The sum of the numbers on opposite faces of each die is always 7. What would the tower look like from behind?

solutions.title: Opposite faces
solutions.body:
From behind we see the faces opposite to the front faces, and left and right are swapped.
- Front faces: left die 5, bottom middle 3, top die 3, right die 2.
- Back faces: $7 - 5 = 2$, $7 - 3 = 4$, $7 - 3 = 4$, $7 - 2 = 5$.

So from behind: top die 4, bottom row from left to right 5, 4, 2 (the right die now appears on the left). The tops still show 1. Only picture (C) shows this.

**Answer: (C)**

solutions.title: Rule out by one die
solutions.body:
Look only at the die that was on the right with 2 at the front: from behind it is on the left and shows 5. Then check the middle bottom die, which must show 4 from behind, and the far-right die, which must show 2. Only (C) has all of these.

**Answer: (C)**

prompt: You can place together the cards pictured, to make different three digit numbers, for instance 989 or 986. How many different three digit numbers can you make with these cards?

solutions.title: Turn the cards
solutions.body:
The cards are 6, 8 and 9, and a 6 turned upside down is a 9 (and the other way round). So two of the cards can each show 6 or 9; the 8 is always 8.
- The 8 can be in 3 places.
- Each of the other two places can show 6 or 9: $2 \times 2 = 4$ ways.

$3 \times 4 = 12$ numbers.

**Answer: (E) 12**

prompt: Andrea made the pattern in the picture out of several identical tiles. None of the tiles overlap each other. Which of the following tiles could she definitely not have used?

solutions.title: Count triangles
solutions.body:
The pattern is three hexagons, each made of 6 small triangles: 18 triangles. The tiles have (A) 6, (B) 2, (C) 6, (D) 5 and (E) 3 triangles. Identical tiles must split 18 evenly, and 18 cannot be split into 5s. So tile (D) is impossible.

**Answer: (D)**

solutions.title: Check that the others fit
solutions.body:
(A): 3 hexagons. (B): each hexagon is 3 rhombi. (E): each hexagon is 2 trapezoids. (C) can also be placed 3 times. Only (D), with 5 triangles, cannot work because $18 \div 5$ is not whole.

**Answer: (D)**

prompt: The picture shows a fortress made from cubes. How many cubes were used to make it?

solutions.title: Wall plus towers
solutions.body:
The wall goes round a square that is 7 cubes long on each side. One layer of the wall has $7 + 7 + 5 + 5 = 24$ cubes. The wall is 2 layers high: $48$ cubes. On top stand 8 single cubes (the battlements). Total $48 + 8 = 56$.

**Answer: (A) 56**

solutions.title: Subtract the hole
solutions.body:
A full $7 \times 7$ layer has 49 cubes; the empty middle is $5 \times 5 = 25$, so the ring has $49 - 25 = 24$ cubes. Two layers: 48, plus 8 battlement cubes: 56.

**Answer: (A) 56**

prompt: Johannes wrote the numbers 6, 7 and 8 in the circles as shown. He wants to write the numbers 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5 in the remaining circles so that the sum of the numbers along each side of the square is 13. What will be the sum of the numbers in the grey circles?

solutions.title: Fill in the circles
solutions.body:
8 is in the top-left corner, 6 in the middle of the right side and 7 in the middle of the bottom side. Call the other corners top-right $a$, bottom-right $b$, bottom-left $c$.
- Right side: $a + 6 + b = 13$, so $a + b = 7$.
- Bottom side: $c + 7 + b = 13$, so $b + c = 6$.
- Top side: $8 + (\text{top middle}) + a = 13$, so top middle $= 5 - a$.

Trying the numbers 1–5: $a = 2$, $b = 5$, $c = 1$, top middle 3, left middle 4 works. The grey circles are the four corners: $8 + 2 + 5 + 1 = 16$.

**Answer: (E) 16**

solutions.title: Add all four sides
solutions.body:
Adding the four sides gives $4 \times 13 = 52$. This counts the middle circles once and the corners twice. All eight numbers add up to $1 + 2 + 3 + 4 + 5 + 6 + 7 + 8 = 36$. So the corners are counted once more: corners $= 52 - 36 = 16$.

**Answer: (E) 16**

prompt: Sylvia draws patterns with hexagons as shown. If she carries on drawing in this way, how many hexagons will there be in the fifth pattern?

solutions.title: Add a ring each time
solutions.body:
The patterns have 1, 7 and 19 hexagons. Each new pattern adds a ring around the old one: 6, 12, 18, 24, ... hexagons. Pattern 4: $19 + 18 = 37$. Pattern 5: $37 + 24 = 61$.

**Answer: (D) 61**

prompt: In which of the five pictures is the white area bigger than the grey area?

solutions.title: Check each picture for halves
solutions.body:
- (A): each grey triangle has a matching white triangle → grey = white.
- (B): two grey and two white triangles of the same size → equal.
- (C): 2 grey and 2 white small squares → equal.
- (E): the grey parts again make exactly half.
- (D): only **two small** grey triangles, each $\frac{1}{8}$ of the square, so grey $= \frac{1}{4}$ and white $= \frac{3}{4}$.

**Answer: (D)**

solutions.title: Look at picture (D) closely
solutions.body:
The horizontal line cuts the square into two halves. The diagonal line cuts each half into a small triangle and a bigger piece. In each half only the small triangle (a quarter of that half) is grey. So the grey part is much smaller than the white part.

**Answer: (D)**

prompt: Barbara wrote the word MATHEMATIC on a piece of paper. She used the same colour for letters which are the same. She used a different colour for letters which are different. How many different colours did she use?

solutions.title: List the different letters
solutions.body:
Write each letter only the first time it appears: M, A, T, H, E, I, C.

That is **7** different letters, so 7 colours.

**Answer: (A) 7**

solutions.title: Count and remove repeats
solutions.body:
MATHEMATIC has 10 letters. M, A and T each appear twice, so there are 3 repeats: $10 - 3 = 7$.

**Answer: (A) 7**

prompt: Father hangs towels on the washing line as shown in the picture. For three towels he uses 4 clothes pegs. How many clothes pegs would he use for 5 towels?

solutions.title: Neighbours share a peg
solutions.body:
Two towels next to each other share one peg. So there is one peg at the start and then one more peg after each towel: $1 + 5 = 6$.

**Answer: (C) 6**

solutions.title: Continue the pattern
solutions.body:
1 towel → 2 pegs, 2 towels → 3 pegs, 3 towels → 4 pegs. Each new towel needs 1 more peg, so 4 towels → 5 pegs and 5 towels → 6 pegs.

**Answer: (C) 6**

prompt: Oli coloured in the following 8 fields in the grid: A2, B1, B2, B3, B4, C3, D3 and D4. Which is his grid?

solutions.title: Use the whole column B
solutions.body:
B1, B2, B3 and B4 means the whole column B is coloured. Only grid (C) has all of column B grey. Check the rest of (C): A2 is grey, C3 and D3 are grey, D4 is grey — exactly the list.

**Answer: (C)**

solutions.title: Rule out grids
solutions.body:
- (A) has C1 coloured, which is not in the list.
- (B) has B1 white.
- (D) has C1 and D1 coloured.
- (E) has B1 white.

Only (C) is left, and it matches all 8 fields.

**Answer: (C)**

prompt: 13 children play hide and seek. One of them searches. After a little while 9 children are found. How many are still hiding?

solutions.title: Take away the seeker first
solutions.body:
One child searches, so $13 - 1 = 12$ children hide. 9 of them are found: $12 - 9 = 3$ are still hiding.

**Answer: (A) 3**

solutions.title: Add up
solutions.body:
Seeker + found + still hiding = 13, so $1 + 9 + ? = 13$, which gives $? = 3$.

**Answer: (A) 3**

prompt: Mike and Jake play darts. Each of them throws three darts, as shown in the picture. Who won, and by how many points?

choices.text: Mike won. He had three points more.
Jake won. He had 4 points more.
Mike won. He had 2 points more.
Jake won. He had 2 points more.
Mike won. He had 4 points more.

solutions.title: Add each score
solutions.body:
Mike's darts are in 25, 35 and 7: $25 + 35 + 7 = 67$.

Jake's darts are in 3, 15 and 45: $3 + 15 + 45 = 63$.

$67 - 63 = 4$, so Mike won by 4 points.

**Answer: (E)**

solutions.title: Compare dart by dart
solutions.body:
Pair the darts: Mike's 25 vs Jake's 15 (+10 for Mike), Mike's 35 vs Jake's 45 (−10 for Mike), Mike's 7 vs Jake's 3 (+4 for Mike). In total Mike is $10 - 10 + 4 = 4$ points ahead.

**Answer: (E)**

prompt: A wall was tiled alternately with grey and striped tiles. Some tiles have fallen from the wall. How many grey tiles have fallen off?

solutions.title: Continue the checkerboard
solutions.body:
Grey and striped tiles alternate in every row and every column, like a chessboard. Fill in the hole row by row:

- Row 2: two tiles are missing; the first one is grey → 1 grey.
- Row 3: five tiles are missing: grey, striped, grey, striped, grey → 3 grey.
- Row 4: six tiles are missing: grey, striped, grey, striped, grey, striped → 3 grey.

$1 + 3 + 3 = 7$.

**Answer: (C) 7**

solutions.title: Count all and subtract
solutions.body:
The wall is 8 tiles long and 5 tiles high: 40 tiles. In a chessboard pattern half of them, 20, are grey. Counting the grey tiles still on the wall gives 13, so $20 - 13 = 7$ grey tiles fell off.

**Answer: (C) 7**

prompt: On the 24th February 2012 Grandfather's chicks hatched. There are 29 days in February in 2012. How old are the chicks today on 15th March 2012?

solutions.title: Count the days in two parts
solutions.body:
From 24 February to 29 February: $29 - 24 = 5$ days. Then from 29 February to 15 March: 15 days. Total $5 + 15 = 20$ days.

**Answer: (D) 20 days**

solutions.title: Count back from 15 March
solutions.body:
15 days back from 15 March is the last day of February (29 February). The chicks hatched 5 days before that (25, 26, 27, 28, 29 February → 24 February). $15 + 5 = 20$ days.

**Answer: (D) 20 days**

prompt: Anna has made two L shapes out of 8 squares (each L shape is made of 4 squares, as shown at the top). How many of the following 4 shapes can she make with both L shapes?

solutions.title: Split each shape
solutions.body:
Try to cut every shape into two L pieces of 4 squares:

- The 2 × 4 rectangle: an L standing up on the left and an upside-down L on the right fit together.
- The second shape: the left column of 3 with the bottom square next to it is one L; the middle column of 3 with the square sticking out on the right is the other.
- The third shape: the top row of 3 with the square below its left end is one L; the column of 3 below with the square at the bottom right is the other.
- The fourth shape: the top 3 squares of the tall column with the square to the right of the third one form one L; the bottom row of 3 with the square above its right end is the other.

All **4** shapes work.

**Answer: (E) 4**

solutions.title: Each shape is two Ls
solutions.body:
All four shapes have 8 squares, which is right for two Ls. Turning and flipping an L allowed, you can find an L of 4 squares in each shape such that the 4 squares left over also form an L. Since none of the shapes fails, the answer is all 4.

**Answer: (E) 4**

prompt: 3 balloons cost 12 cents more than 1 balloon. How much does 1 balloon cost?

solutions.title: Two extra balloons
solutions.body:
3 balloons are 2 balloons more than 1 balloon. So 2 balloons cost 12 cents, and 1 balloon costs $12 \div 2 = 6$ cents.

**Answer: (B) 6 cents**

solutions.title: Check the choices
solutions.body:
If a balloon costs 6 cents: 3 balloons cost 18 cents, and $18 - 6 = 12$. ✓

**Answer: (B) 6 cents**

prompt: Grandmother baked 20 ginger biscuits for her grandchildren. She decorated them with raisins and nuts. First she decorated 15 with raisins, and then 15 with nuts. No biscuit was left over. How many biscuits were decorated with both raisins and nuts?

solutions.title: Count the extra decorations
solutions.body:
$15 + 15 = 30$ decorations went on 20 biscuits. Every biscuit got at least one. The $30 - 20 = 10$ extra decorations are on biscuits that got both.

**Answer: (E) 10**

solutions.title: Biscuits without raisins
solutions.body:
$20 - 15 = 5$ biscuits got no raisins, so they must have nuts (none is left over). The other $15 - 5 = 10$ biscuits with nuts also have raisins.

**Answer: (E) 10**

prompt: In the school for animals there are 3 cats, 2 ducks, 2 sheep and some dogs. The teacher counted the legs of all the animals, and got 44. How many dogs go to the school?

solutions.title: Subtract the known legs
solutions.body:
Cats: $3 \times 4 = 12$, ducks: $2 \times 2 = 4$, sheep: $2 \times 4 = 8$. Together 24 legs. The dogs have $44 - 24 = 20$ legs, so there are $20 \div 4 = 5$ dogs.

**Answer: (B) 5**

prompt: You need 3 pieces to build this shape. Each piece is made out of 4 equally sized cubes of the same colour. What is the shape of the white piece?

solutions.title: Find all 12 cubes
solutions.body:
The block is 2 cubes wide, 3 deep and 2 high: 12 cubes, 4 of each colour.

- Light grey we can see: both front top cubes, the front bottom right cube and the middle bottom right cube → 4.
- Dark grey we can see: the back top row, the middle top right cube and the back bottom right cube → 4.
- White we can see: the front bottom left cube and the middle top left cube. The other two white cubes must be the hidden ones: middle bottom left and back bottom left.

So the white piece is a row of 3 cubes (bottom left, front to back) with one cube on top of the middle one.

**Answer: (D)**

solutions.title: Rule out the others
solutions.body:
The white piece contains the front bottom left cube and the cube on top of the middle left position, so it has a cube sitting on top of the middle of a row of three. (A), (B), (C) and (E) do not have that shape; (D) does.

**Answer: (D)**

prompt: 15 tables were set for a party. 5 plates were laid on 6 tables. 3 plates were laid on the rest of the tables. How many plates were needed in total?

solutions.title: Two groups of tables
solutions.body:
$6 \times 5 = 30$ plates. The other $15 - 6 = 9$ tables get $9 \times 3 = 27$ plates. Total $30 + 27 = 57$.

**Answer: (C) 57**

solutions.title: Start with 3 everywhere
solutions.body:
Put 3 plates on all 15 tables: 45 plates. The 6 big tables need 2 more each: $6 \times 2 = 12$. Total $45 + 12 = 57$.

**Answer: (C) 57**

prompt: A flea stands on the floor and wants to climb the 10 steps. He can either jump 3 steps upwards or jump 4 steps downwards. What is the smallest number of jumps he must make? (In the picture, "Boden" means floor and "Stufe" means step.)

solutions.title: Up and down jumps
solutions.body:
Going only up: 3, 6, 9, 12, ... never hits 10. Every down jump takes away 4, so we need $3 \times (\text{up}) - 4 \times (\text{down}) = 10$.

- 1 down jump: up jumps must give 14 — not a multiple of 3.
- 2 down jumps: up jumps must give 18 = 6 jumps of 3. ✓

That is $6 + 2 = 8$ jumps, e.g. 3, 6, 9, 12, 8, 11, 14, 10.

**Answer: (E) 8**

solutions.title: Look at the remainders
solutions.body:
After 1, 2, 3, ... up jumps you are on step 3, 6, 9, 12, 15, 18. A down jump changes the step by 4. From 18, two down jumps reach 10. Fewer up jumps don't work: from 12 you would reach 8 or 4, from 15 you reach 11 or 7. So the fewest jumps is $6 + 2 = 8$.

**Answer: (E) 8**

prompt: Frank laid out his dominoes as shown in the picture. (Dominoes which touch must always have the same number of points.) Before his brother George removed two dominoes there were 33 points altogether. How many points is the question mark worth?

solutions.title: Add what you can see
solutions.body:
The visible dominoes are 1|0, 0|5, 5|3, 3|2 and 1|2, with $1 + 0 + 0 + 5 + 5 + 3 + 3 + 2 + 1 + 2 = 22$ points. The two missing dominoes have $33 - 22 = 11$ points.

Because touching halves match, they are 2|? and ?|1. So $2 + ? + ? + 1 = 11$, which means $? + ? = 8$ and $? = 4$.

**Answer: (C) 4**

solutions.title: Check
solutions.body:
With ? = 4 the missing dominoes are 2|4 and 4|1: $2 + 4 + 4 + 1 = 11$, and $22 + 11 = 33$. ✓

**Answer: (C) 4**

prompt: In an arithmetic-sudoku, the values 1, 2, 3, 4 appear exactly once in each row and each column. Which value belongs in the grey square?

solutions.title: Work out the calculations first
solutions.body:
The grid becomes:

- Row 1: 1, _, 3, _
- Row 2: 4, 3, _, 1
- Row 3: 3, 4, 1, _
- Row 4: 2, 1, _, grey

Column 3 already has 3 and 1, row 2 needs a 2 there, so row 4 column 3 is 4. Row 4 then has 2, 1, 4, so the grey square is **3**.

**Answer: (C) 3**

solutions.title: Use the last column
solutions.body:
Last column: row 2 is 1. Row 3 has 3, 4, 1, so its last cell is 2. Row 1 has 1 and 3 and its second cell must be 2 (column 2 has 3, 4, 1), so row 1 ends with 4. Column 4 now has 4, 1, 2 — the grey cell is 3.

**Answer: (C) 3**

prompt: The classmates of Thomas are twice as many girls as boys. How many children could be in the class?

solutions.title: Don't forget Thomas
solutions.body:
Thomas's classmates are everyone except Thomas. Among them, for every boy there are 2 girls, so the number of classmates is a multiple of 3 (1 + 2 = 3). The whole class is classmates **plus Thomas**: a multiple of 3, plus 1.

- 30, 24: multiples of 3 (no).
- 20 → 19 classmates, 29 → 28 classmates: not multiples of 3.
- 25 → 24 classmates = 8 boys + 16 girls. ✓

**Answer: (D) 25**

solutions.title: Build a class
solutions.body:
Try 8 boy classmates and 16 girl classmates. With Thomas there are $8 + 16 + 1 = 25$ children. No other choice is "one more than a multiple of 3".

**Answer: (D) 25**

prompt: Gregory made two 3-digit numbers from the numbers 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6. Each number was used only once. Afterwards he added the numbers together. What is the largest answer that he could have got?

solutions.title: Biggest digits in the biggest places
solutions.body:
The hundreds digits count 100 times, so use 6 and 5 there. Then 4 and 3 for the tens, and 2 and 1 for the ones: e.g. $642 + 531 = 1173$.

**Answer: (D) 1173**

solutions.title: Place values
solutions.body:
Sum $= 100 \times (6+5) + 10 \times (4+3) + (2+1) = 1100 + 70 + 3 = 1173$. 1221 is impossible because the hundreds can give at most 1100 and the rest at most $70 + 3$.

**Answer: (D) 1173**

prompt: Anna, Laura, Lisa and Katharina wanted to take a photo together. Anna and Katharina are best friends and wanted to stand next to each other. Lisa also wanted to stand next to Anna. In how many different ways can the photo be taken, if their wishes are to be met?

solutions.title: Anna in the middle of a group
solutions.body:
Anna needs Katharina and Lisa both next to her, so the three stand as Lisa–Anna–Katharina or Katharina–Anna–Lisa. Laura stands on the left or on the right of this group: $2 \times 2 = 4$ ways.

**Answer: (B) 4**

solutions.body:
With L = Laura, S = Lisa, A = Anna, K = Katharina:

- L S A K
- L K A S
- S A K L
- K A S L

4 ways.

**Answer: (B) 4**

prompt: Grandma's watch has an hour, minute and second hand. We don't know which hand does which job, but we know that the watch tells the correct time. At 12:55:30 hours the watch looked as pictured. How will the watch look at 8:11:00 hours?

solutions.title: Find out which hand is which
solutions.body:
At 12:55:30: the second hand points at 6 (30 seconds), the minute hand points just past 11 (55 minutes), and the hour hand is almost at 1. In the picture, the short hand pointing down is the second hand, the hand pointing to 11 is the minute hand and the hand near 1 is the hour hand.

At 8:11:00: the second hand (short) points at 12, the minute hand points just past 2 (11 minutes), and the hour hand points just past 8. Only picture (E) shows this.

**Answer: (E)**

solutions.title: Rule out pictures
solutions.body:
At 8:11:00 the seconds are 0, so the hand that was at 6 must point straight up at 12, and one hand must point a bit past 2 (11 minutes) with the hand that was near 1 pointing at about 8. The longest hand (the minute hand, at 11 in the first picture) must point a bit past 2. In (A) and (C) the longest hand points at 8, and in (B) the long hand points at 12. In (D) the hand pointing towards 8 is too short — it should be the medium-length hour hand. (E) fits.

prompt: Michael thought of a number. He multiplied this number with itself, added 1, multiplied the result by 10, added 3 and multiplied the total by 4. He arrived at 2012. Which number had Michael thought of to start with?

A rectangular piece of paper is 60 mm long and 36 mm wide. After making a straight cut you have a square and a leftover piece. You do the same with the leftover piece and so on until the leftover piece itself is square. What is the side length of the last square?

solutions.title: Cut step by step
solutions.body:
- 60 × 36: cut a 36 × 36 square, left 24 × 36.
- 24 × 36: cut a 24 × 24 square, left 24 × 12.
- 24 × 12: cut a 12 × 12 square, left 12 × 12 — a square!

**Answer: (E) 12 mm**

solutions.title: Common measure
solutions.body:
Each cut takes the shorter side away from the longer one, so both sides stay multiples of any length that measures both 60 and 36. The biggest length that divides both 60 and 36 is 12, and the process ends exactly there.

**Answer: (E) 12 mm**

prompt: In football you get 3 points for a win, no points for a loss, and 1 point for a draw. A team has played 36 matches and has 80 points. What is the maximum number of matches the team could have lost?

solutions.title: Win as much as possible
solutions.body:
To lose many games, the team should get its 80 points in as few games as possible, so it should win as often as it can. $26 \times 3 = 78$, and 2 draws add 2 points: 80 points in $26 + 2 = 28$ games. The other $36 - 28 = 8$ games were lost.

(27 wins would be 81 points — too many.)

**Answer: (E) 8**

solutions.title: Check a bigger number
solutions.body:
Could the team lose 9 games? Then 80 points come from 27 games. Even 27 wins give 81 and any draw instead of a win loses 2 points, giving 79, 77, ... — never 80. So 8 is the maximum.

**Answer: (E) 8**

prompt: How many more bricks does the right hand pyramid have than the left hand pyramid?

solutions.title: Count row by row
solutions.body:
Left pyramid: $1 + 2 + 3 + 4 = 10$ bricks. Right pyramid: $1 + 2 + 3 + 4 + 5 = 15$ bricks. $15 - 10 = 5$.

solutions.title: Only the extra row
solutions.body:
The right pyramid is the left pyramid with one more row of 5 bricks at the bottom, so it has 5 more bricks.

**Answer: (B) 5**

prompt: In which picture are there more black kangaroos than white ones?

solutions.body:
Cross out one black and one white kangaroo together until one colour runs out. In (D) two black kangaroos are left over; in every other picture the pairing ends with no black kangaroo left.

prompt:

solutions.body:
Both numbers are the same, so each is half of 104: $104 \div 2 = 52$. The hidden digit is 2.

prompt: Five children are talking about the number 325. Andreas: "It is a three digit number."; Boris: "All the digits are different." Sara: "The digit sum is 10." Gerda: "The units digit is 5." Daniela: "All the digits are odd." Who has made a mistake?

prompt: Anna starts in the direction of the arrow. At each crossing she turns either right or left. At the first crossing she turns right, at the next left, then left again, then right, then left and left again. What will she find at the next crossing that she comes to?

solutions.title: Follow the path
solutions.body:
Anna walks up the middle street.

1. First crossing: right → she walks to the right.
2. Next crossing: left → up.
3. Next crossing (the cat): left → to the left.
4. Next crossing: right → up.
5. Next crossing (the dog): left → to the left.
6. Next crossing (the car): left → down.

The next crossing below the car is where the doll is.

**Answer: (A)**

solutions.title: Use coordinates
solutions.body:
Number the vertical streets 1, 2, 3 from the left and the horizontal streets 1, 2, 3 from the bottom. Anna starts on vertical street 2. Her crossings are (2,1) → (3,1) → (3,2) → (2,2) → (2,3) → (1,3), and after turning left at (1,3) she walks down to (1,2), where the doll sits.

**Answer: (A)**

prompt: Nathalie wanted to build a large cube out of lots of small cubes, just like in picture 1. How many cubes are missing from picture 2 that would be needed to build the large cube?

solutions.title: Count layer by layer
solutions.body:
The big cube has $3 \times 3 \times 3 = 27$ small cubes. In picture 2:

- Bottom layer: all 9 cubes are there.
- Middle layer: the two cubes in the front-right and middle-right corner are missing → 7 cubes.
- Top layer: only the 3 cubes on the left side and the back cube next to them are there → 4 cubes.

$9 + 7 + 4 = 20$ cubes, so $27 - 20 = 7$ are missing.

**Answer: (C) 7**

solutions.title: Count the missing ones directly
solutions.body:
Middle layer: 2 missing. Top layer: $9 - 4 = 5$ missing. Total $2 + 5 = 7$.

**Answer: (C) 7**

prompt: The rectangular mirror has broken. Which piece is missing?

solutions.title: Look at the gap
solutions.body:
The gap is at the bottom left corner of the mirror. It has 4 sides: a short piece of the left edge and a longer piece of the bottom edge, which meet at a **right angle** (the corner of the mirror), and two long cracks that meet at the point where all the cracks start.

Piece (B) has exactly this shape: 4 sides, one right angle between a short and a longer side, and two long slanted sides meeting in a sharp point.

**Answer: (B)**

prompt: How many triangles can be seen in the picture on the right? (Be careful! A triangle can be also be made by joining several smaller triangles together.)

solutions.title: Small ones, then big ones
solutions.body:
- Small triangles: 3 in the top row and 5 in the bottom row = 8.
- Big triangles made of 4 small ones: one with its top at the upper left corner and one with its top at the upper right corner = 2.

No bigger triangles fit. $8 + 2 = 10$.

**Answer: (B) 10**

solutions.title: Count by top corner
solutions.body:
Every upward triangle has a top corner. Top corners in the upper row of points give 2 small + 2 big triangles; top corners in the middle row give 3 small ones. Downward small triangles: 1 in the top row and 2 in the bottom row. $4 + 3 + 3 = 10$.

**Answer: (B) 10**

prompt: Vera's Mum has made sandwiches, each using two slices of bread. There are 24 slices in a pack. How many sandwiches can she make with two whole and one half packets of bread?

solutions.title: Count the slices
solutions.body:
Two packs: 48 slices. Half a pack: 12 slices. Together 60 slices, which make $60 \div 2 = 30$ sandwiches.

**Answer: (D) 30**

solutions.title: Sandwiches per pack
solutions.body:
One pack makes $24 \div 2 = 12$ sandwiches, half a pack makes 6. $12 + 12 + 6 = 30$.

**Answer: (D) 30**

prompt: Daniel had 36 sweets. He shared them equally between his siblings. How many siblings can he definitely not have?

solutions.title: Check which numbers divide 36
solutions.body:
$36 \div 2 = 18$, $36 \div 3 = 12$, $36 \div 4 = 9$, $36 \div 6 = 6$ all work. $36 \div 5$ does not: 5 × 7 = 35 leaves 1 sweet over.

**Answer: (D) 5**

solutions.title: Multiples of 5
solutions.body:
If 36 sweets could be shared among 5 children, 36 would be in the 5 times table — but numbers in the 5 times table end in 0 or 5.

**Answer: (D) 5**

prompt: Pinocchio's nose is 9 cm long. If he lies his nose grows by 6 cm. If he tells the truth it shortens by 2 cm. He tells three untruths and twice the truth. How long is Pinocchio's nose now?

solutions.title: Add and subtract
solutions.body:
Three lies: $3 \times 6 = 18$ cm longer. Two truths: $2 \times 2 = 4$ cm shorter. $9 + 18 - 4 = 23$ cm.

**Answer: (D) 23 cm**

solutions.title: Step by step
solutions.body:
9 → 15 → 21 → 27 (three lies) → 25 → 23 (two truths). The order does not matter.

**Answer: (D) 23 cm**

prompt: Which of the following pieces can be joined to the one pictured so that a rectangle is formed?

solutions.title: Fill the gaps
solutions.body:
Think of the pictured piece on a grid. It is 4 squares wide; its columns are 4, 2, 3 and 2 squares tall. To make a rectangle 4 wide and 5 tall, the piece on top has to fill a row of 4 on top plus the gaps of 2, 1 and 2 squares above the low columns.

Piece (B), turned on its side, has exactly this shape: a long row of 4 with bumps of 2, 1 and 2 squares (the notch in (B) fits over the column of height 3).

**Answer: (B)**

solutions.title: Count squares
solutions.body:
The pictured piece has $4 + 2 + 3 + 2 = 11$ squares. Piece (B) has 9 squares, and $11 + 9 = 20 = 4 \times 5$, the size of the rectangle. Trying the other pieces in every position always leaves a hole or a bump sticking out.

**Answer: (B)**

prompt: In a shop you can buy oranges in bags of 4 or bags of 10. Pedro wants to buy exactly 48 oranges. What is the smallest number of bags he must buy?

solutions.title: Use as many 10s as possible
solutions.body:
4 bags of 10 give 40 oranges, and the 8 missing oranges are 2 bags of 4: $40 + 8 = 48$ with 6 bags. With 5 bags you can get 44 (4 tens, 1 four) or 50 (5 tens), but never exactly 48. So the smallest number is 6.

**Answer: (C) 6**

solutions.title: Why not 5 bags?
solutions.body:
With 5 bags: if $t$ are bags of 10, the total is $10t + 4(5 - t) = 20 + 6t$. For 48 we'd need $6t = 28$, which is impossible. 4 bags hold at most 40. So 6 bags is the minimum.

**Answer: (C) 6**

prompt: At the London 2012 Olympic games the USA won the most medals: 46 Gold, 29 Silver and 29 Bronze medals. China was second with 38 Gold, 27 Silver and 23 Bronze medals. How many more medals did the USA win than China?
30 children took part in a sports competition, in the sports football and handball. 15 took part in football and 20 took part in handball. How many students took part in both sports?

solutions.title: Count twice, subtract
solutions.body:
$15 + 20 = 35$, but there are only 30 children. The $35 - 30 = 5$ children who were counted twice played both sports.

**Answer: (E) 5**

solutions.title: Only handball
solutions.body:
$30 - 15 = 15$ children did not play football, so they played only handball. Handball had 20 players, so $20 - 15 = 5$ also played football.

**Answer: (E) 5**

prompt: The number 35 has the property that it can be divided by its unit digit, because 35 divided by 5 is exactly 7. The number 38 does not have this property. How many numbers bigger than 21, but smaller than 30 have this property?

solutions.title: Think of the 20
solutions.body:
A number $20 + d$ is divisible by $d$ exactly when 20 is divisible by $d$. For $d$ from 2 to 9, 20 is divisible by 2, 4 and 5 only → 3 numbers.

**Answer: (B) 3**

prompt: In February 2013 Schnurrli the tomcat slept for exactly three weeks. For how many hours in this month was he awake?

solutions.title: Days awake
solutions.body:
February 2013 has 28 days. Three weeks are 21 days, so he was awake for 7 days = $7 \times 24 = 168$ hours.

**Answer: (A) 168**

solutions.title: One week
solutions.body:
28 days are exactly 4 weeks. Asleep 3 weeks means awake 1 week = 168 hours.

**Answer: (A) 168**

prompt: Andi, Betti, Clara and Dani were born in the same year. Their birthdays are on the 20th February, 12th April, 12th May and 25th May, but not necessarily in that order. Betti and Andi were born in the same month. Andi and Clara were born on the same day in different months. Who is the oldest?

choices.text: There is not enough information to answer the question.

solutions.title: Use the clues
solutions.body:
Only May has two birthdays, so Betti and Andi were born in May (12th and 25th). Andi shares the day number with Clara, so Andi is 12 May and Clara is 12 April. Betti is 25 May, and Dani is 20 February — the earliest date, so Dani is the oldest.

**Answer: (D) Dani**

solutions.title: Who is left?
solutions.body:
Andi and Betti take the two May dates, and Clara must have the 12th in another month — 12 April. Dani gets 20 February, the earliest birthday in the year.

**Answer: (D) Dani**

prompt: If I join the midpoints of the sides of the large triangle in the picture, a small triangle is formed. If I join the midpoints of the sides of this small triangle, a tiny triangle is formed. How many of these tiny triangles can fit into the largest triangle at the same time?

solutions.title: Each step makes quarters
solutions.body:
